speakeroldname: Mr. Barnett J. Danson (Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: GUIDELINES FOR USE OF GOVERNMENT AIRCRAFT DURING ELECTION CAMPAIGNS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, guidelines governing the use of official aircraft by ministers during an election campaign were issued in May 1968 by the Prime Minister, and these still prevail.
Official aircraft may not be used for purposes related to the election campaign. This means not merely that government business must be involved in any such journey, but that official aircraft may be used only when the performance of government business is the sole public purpose of the trip. Therefore, governmental aircraft should not be used in cases where the minister, or party concerned, will be engaging in any public political activities even if the trip also involves some government business.

1.	Did Canada oppose (a) General Principle Two (b) General Principle Three (c) General Principle Seven (d) General Principle Eight adopted by UNCTAD I and listed in the "final act" of that conference and, if so, for what reasons?
2.	Did Canada abstain from voting on (a) General Principle Four (b) General Principle Five (c) General Principle Eleven (d) General Principle Twelve (e) General Principle Fourteen (f) General Principle Fifteen and, if so, for what reasons?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
1 (a) Yes, Canada opposed General Principle Two because it called for the adoption of trading methods to eliminate discrimination based on socio-economic systems. This principle was put forward by the Soviet bloc which sought to eliminate all reference to trade restrictions based on strategic grounds, (b) Yes, Canada opposed General Principle Three regarding the sovereign right of each country freely to trade with other countries and freely to dispose of its natural resources because this right was not qualified by any reference to international law, to agreements freely entered into, or to relevant UNGA resolutions. (c) Yes. While Canada had no difficulty with that section of General Principle Seven which dealt with access to markets, we opposed the concept of stabilization

of commodity prices at artificial levels and the relating of those price levels to those of manufactured goods, (d) Yes. General Principle Eight sought to deal with the application of the most favoured nation principle to the question of tariff preferences for developing countries. At that time Canada was unable to accept this principle. Canada is, of course, among those developed countries which subsequently accepted the Generalized Preference Scheme established at UNCTAD II.
2 (a), (b), (c) and (d). Yes. While often sympathetic to the general tenets of these Principles, Canada could not, at that time, accept the phraseology which was in many cases unbalanced and arbitrary. For example, Principles Fifteen and Four concerned respectively the special needs of the least developed of the developing countries, and the requirement for all nations to pledge themselves to pursue policies designed to accelerate economic growth. The Canadian abstention in both cases reflected difficulty with the uncompromising text rather than disagreement on substance. Delegations of other major trading nations, including Canada, were likewise unable to envisage that national policies could feasibly be directed towards a completely new international division of labour (General Principle Five). Canada, together with other major aid donors, could not accept that there should be no element of discretion in the choice of aid recipients (Principle Eleven), that UNCTAD should prejudge the conclusion of an agreement on general and complete disarmament (Principle Twelve) or the implication that the colonial period had brought no economic benefit to developing countries (Principle Fourteen).

1.	By what means is the government presently preventing pollution of the Great Lakes?

speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of the Environment and Transport as follows: 1. The Federal Government is preventing pollution through the application of anti-pollution legislation, such as the Fisheries Act, the Canada Water Act and the Canada Shipping Act, and through such agreements as the Canada/United States Agreement and the Canada/Ontario Agreement. The Department of Transport enforces the Oil Pollution Prevention Regulations and the Garbage Pollution Prevention Regulations throughout the Great Lakes. These

Regulations apply to ships and both carry a possible fine of $100,000 against offenders. Marine surveyors employed by the Department of Transport investigate reports of infractions of these regulations and lay charges whenever necessary. Coast Guard vessels employed by the Department of Transport carry out regular surveillance in Great Lakes waters. A Coast Guard aircraft with departmental surveyors acting as observers also carries out regular anti-pollution patrols throughout the area.
2.	The Garbage Pollution Prevention Regulations were promulgated specifically to deal with the problem of waste from vessels in the Great Lakes and in other Inland Waters.
3.	No.

Brownridge dealing with an impaired driving charge and refusal to take a breathalyzer test. speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: JUDGMENT ASSERTING RIGHT OF ACCUSED TO CONSULT COUNSEL BEFORE BREATHALYZER TEST FOR IMPAIRED DRIVING-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no present intention to undertake legislation. The practical matter, I think, is that it is important to have working enforcement in connection with drinking drivers, and the breathalyzer is extremely useful in that regard. I do not at the present time see any inconsistency between that and the decision of the Supreme Court in terms of the ability to contact counsel in certain circumstances. A careful reading of the judgment indicates, I think, the court's concern that this should not interfere with the ordinary taking of breathalyzer tests. The only case I can see for further legislation is if there is uncertainty about

the extent of the right and the period of time which could be taken up in consultation with counsel.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Orders of the day.
The House resumed, from Tuesday, June 27, consideration of Bill C-183, to amend the Canada Labour Code, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lincoln M. Alexander (Hamilton West) moved:
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSION AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
That Bill C-183, to amend the Canada Labour Code, be amended by deleting lines 33 to 39 on page 3 thereof and by substituting therefor:
"(ii) entitled to receive remuneration for driving the vehicle in addition to and separate from the amount he is paid for providing the vehicle, and"

He said: Mr. Speaker, the gist of this motion is to register some concern about the fact that one result of the subclause which defines dependent contractor may be the demise of the independent contractor. This subclause of the bill as presently drafted appears to be the only attempt to differentiate between independent and dependent contractors, and is based on a common purchasing arrangement which does not take into account two distinct situations.
I would like to point out the situations of which I believe the government was not fully aware when drafting this bill which, of course, deals with the owners of trucks or the drivers of trucks, as the case may be. There are two distinct situations. The first is the truck which is owned and operated by a company. The problem arises in the second situation. This is where the same company is employing trucks, owned or leased and operated by persons on a contractual basis. In this regard, we have to ascertain who, in fact, is a dependent contractor and who is an independent contractor. I find no qualms with respect to giving the opportunity to a dependent contractor to become involved with this act but the subclause is drafted in vague generalities.
The purpose of this amendment is to at least clarify the difference between a dependent contractor, who in fact receives remuneration for the operation of his truck plus a further sum for the use of his driver, and an independent contractor who is usually paid one sum, whether it is a flat rate per mile or for the use of the truck in these particular circumstances. Although there is no question about the need for this particular subclause in. the definition section, I think it is too broad and we cannot afford the demise of the independent contractor. As a matter of fact, many letters have come to my attention, as well as to the attention of two other members, to the effect that the independent contractor does not like nor does he have the desire to be involved as a driver with drivers of company trucks. One can readily see that a very serious situation can develop when company drivers are involved in union matters or union agencies with independent truckers who drive their own trucks. It is obvious that this can result in some problem.
It has been pointed out to me by the independent contractor that he negotiates his own contract, owns and drives his own trucks, arranges his own maintenance, his hours of work are arranged to suit the operation of the truck and the hours of work, the working conditions and the earnings are not related to carrier-owned trucks or drivers. What I am seeking to do is to clear up cases which involve a contractor working under a contract which entitles him to receive remuneration for driving a vehicle in addition to an amount paid for providing a vehicle. The clause as presently drafted is not clear on this point; it covers common carriers and other employees. The amendment seeks to clarify a complex clause.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSION AND CONCILIATION BOARDS

This subject has been examined again by officials of my department. I have looked at it as well. I appreciate the hon. member having raised it previously in committee where a discussion took place, and again here this morning. He says he sees no difficulty about the provision in
June 30, 1972

principle, but finds it too sweeping and inclusive. On the other side, we think the definition proposed by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) is unduly restrictive. On balance, therefore, I would ask him to accept the best judgment of those familiar with the industry in my department and allow the definition to stand. If we followed the line he is suggesting, it would cover a very small category in our view.
The key to the definition is not really the question of remuneration but the use of the vehicle. If the vehicle is governed by a contract, that is the determining factor, not the manner in which remuneration is received. Undoubtedly, if the labour relations board were asked to determine whether such and such a person was an employee under the terms of this act, that is to say, a dependent contractor, the question would revolve around the use of the vehicle in terms of the contract. It would involve, also, the entitlement of the owner or operator to retain whatever amount was left over after expenses. That amount might, in the ordinary course, be thought of as remuneration but it could be a broader concept. I hope the House will allow us to retain the definition as it now stands.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark Rose (for Mr. Barnett) moved:
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSION AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
That Bill C-183, an act to amend the Canada Labour Code, be amended by deleting from Clause 1, lines 1 to 8 at page 4, and substituting therefor the following:
Canada Labour Code
"(b) a fisherman who is engaged in commercial fishing and accepting or receiving payment, according to the volume and price of fish caught and delivered, from a commercial buyer of fish, whether such fisherman (i) owns and operates his own fishing vessel, provided he as master-owner of a fishing vessel does not employ or engage more than two additional fishermen who share in the proceeds of the fishing voyages, or (ii) shares in the operation of a fishing vessel owned by another person and receives in payment for his services a share or portion of the proceeds of the fishing voyages, or (iii) operates a fishing vessel owned by another person under a rental agreement or conditional sales agreement or any other form of oral or written agreement, or (iv) receives wages for all or part of his employment on a fishing vessel or in fitting out a fishing vessel on which he will be employed."
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am speaking on behalf of my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni in whose name this motion stands. I regret that my hon. friend is not here. He has been very diligent in pursuing this whole question during committee hearings. He has concerned himself with the representations we have heard from the Fishermen's Union and other groups interested in this matter.
It is an important matter to me because a great many fishermen reside in my constituency. Unfortunately however there are far fewer fishermen there now than there were before the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) introduced his new licensing regulations. But that is another question.
A look at the motion reveals the nub of the issue in this case, which is whether or not fishermen can be regarded not as part of some shared venture but as employees for the purpose of this legislation. This question is extremely important to the fishermen. Their national annual income is not very high. It is true many of them work on a share basis, but in many instances they have no alternative. A great number of fishermen are not adequately represented by a union and because of this are forced to work under appalling dangerous conditions at not very remunerative rates at the behest of the large, well-organized, vertically integrated fishing companies. We all know what vertical integration implies. In my view these fishermen are in no way part of a shared venture; they are in fact, employees. The bait-if I may use a fishing term-that is dangled before them in terms of shares is acceptable to them only because up until now for many there has been no reasonable alternative.
During the hearings of the standing committee I was most impressed with the representations made by the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union, and I should like to quote what one witness, Mr. Homer Stevens had to say, as found at page 10:49 of volume 10 of the committee proceedings:
We believe all fishermen, whether they are working aboard vessels owned or operated by fishing companies that are vertically integrated to the point where they own and operate the plants as well as the boats, whether they are employed on vessels owned by other fishermen who deliver under various forms of contract to those same companies or whether fishermen are employed on their own one-man or possibly two-man boats operated in a partnership in which they either own the vessel or are attempting to own it under various kinds of contracts, mortgage contracts or conditional sales agreements-all these should be covered under the new legislation so that the right to bargain collectively would be there to provide equal opportunity to them as with other employees and in order to have their unions certified under the

June 30, 1972
Canada Labour Code
law. This would remove the courts as they are now in the role of sole supreme arbitrator with the power to classify fishermen's unions as illegal conspiracies or during strikes, to state that fishermen are not on strike, that since there is no employer-employee relationship, in their opinion, they are nothing more than illegal conspiracies in defiance of various parts of the common law, with the end result being that fishermen who are attempting to improve their conditions of life, their job opportunities, earnings and so on can find themselves faced with heavy fines, goal sentences, damage suits and all the attendant legal expenses arising out of appeals on that kind of case.
I recognize that exists some doubt whether or not this amendment is constitutionally sound. There are various legal opinions on this and the department, through Mr. Mitchell, expressed one opinion. Various consultations with lawyers held privately by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and others indicated that the constitutional question is not closed at all. The kind of thing envisioned by this amendment would do a great deal to enhance the security and the income of fishermen on both coasts and I think it should be tried.
I think it is well recognized that special provisions are made for fishermen under the unemployment insurance legislation. The reason is that, for the purposes of that legislation, fishermen are recognized as employees not as co-adventurers at all. I do not want to make a long speech on this subject since a great many words have already been said on it already. However, the evidence upholds the validity of UFAWU's argument, and I do not understand why the government tends to be reluctant to embrace this requested definition of an "employee" concept, unless it is because the government is unduly influenced by a strong lobby by the various wealthy fishing companies, though we do not need to use the fingers of both hands to count them since the number in this country is very small and is decreasing.
The position of these companies is virtually one of monopoly, of vertical integration. Therefore, I urge the minister in the strongest terms at my disposal to recognize the rights of these people as employees and to accept the motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. Martin P. O'Connell (Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSION AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose), who is not only giving his own views but those of his colleague from Comox-Alberni. The views of his colleague were very ably and extensively presented to the standing committee. I met at least twice with delegations from the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union and I received representations from the Fisheries Council of British Columbia. In addition, I have had representations from my colleagues on this side of the House, the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Perrault) and the hon. member for Burna-by-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Goode).
There is a very high degree of interest in this question and I have publicly stated I am not unsympathetic to it. In fact, at one point I went further than perhaps I should when I said I thought the fishermen had an unassailable case. But sympathy for a cause does not necessarily make it legal to go further than we are proposing to go. There is no question that the modes of work in the fishing industry are quite varied. Where employees on fishing vessels work for the owner, the situation is clear cut. We have gone

beyond that and made available the benefits of the Labour Code to those who share the cash return, those who are co-adventurers, and this is a significant step forward. However, it still leaves out that group of fishermen who would undoubtedly benefit, as in my view the industry would benefit, from their inclusion in collective bargaining arrangements.
I cannot bring myself to ask this House to pass a provision which, according to the best legal advice that I have been able to get, would be ultra vires the powers of Parliament. We have therefore defined "employee" in such a way as to make available collective bargaining for more members of the fishing industry than has hitherto been the case. We believe that this is within our constitutional jurisdiction.
Although we are sympathetic to, and concerned for, this other group, I cannot ask the House to lead us into an area which in the present circumstances we think would be unconstitutional. There was a very extensive and useful discussion in the standing committee which is on the record, but I must ask my colleagues to let us proceed with the present definition, and to hope that as a result of provincial and federal activity in the future collective bargaining will in fact reach all of the members of this industry.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSION AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to see whether even at this late date I can persuade the minister to ignore the bureaucratic legal advice that he has received and to look at this proposition more favourably. I address myself to him in what I hope is a co-operative plea that he reconsider his position. Let me put this to him. What he has done in the amendment he has proposed is to define the word "employee" as something beyond what an employee is under the common law. He has already taken the legal step which, in effect is that even where there is no employer-employee relationship as recognized in the ordinary law, such people can still come within the scope of the act.
If I may, I assure the minister that what I say is a correct statement because under various labour relations acts in this country, not only the federal act but also the Nova Scotia act, there have been cases before the courts where this has been decided. Without having had time to make a search, I can recall what I always have known as the Lunenburg case in which the courts of Nova Scotia held that co-adventurers such as are described in the amendment the minister has proposed to the bill are not employees. Because they are not employees under the common law, they cannot be considered to be employees under the Nova Scotia Labour Relations Act.
Clearly what the minister has done in the amendment he has proposed with regard to co-adventurers in the fishing industry has been to say in effect that, notwithstanding the fact that these people are not employees in the ordinary legal sense of the word, they are to be recognized as employees for the purpose of this act. I think that is a correct statement of what he has done. They are not employees and the courts have held that. That is not my statement, the courts have held that in the Lunenburg case and in others. They have held that co-adventurers
June 30, 1972

are not employees in the ordinary common law sense of the word. I repeat that what the minister is saying in this proposed law is that although fishermen who share the catch and are co-adventurers in their fishing trip are not employees ordinarily under the law, he makes them employees for the purpose of this act. This is clearly within the powers of the legislature.
What the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) and the United Fishermen's Union say to the minister is simply this, and I ask him to consider it in this light because, with great respect, I think he has misled himself: You are recognizing that a co-ad venturing relationship will be an employee relationship for the purpose of this act. We are saying to you that this only covers a small or large proportion and I really do not know which, of those engaged in the fishing business. There are other situations such as a fishing vessel with an arrangement with a commercial buyer. The commercial buyer will buy all the fish caught by that vessel and the remuneration to the fishermen engaged in the catching will depend on a division of the spoils, and they are usually pretty darn small, which they get from the commercial buyer. That is really what this amendment proposed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni says.
The hon. member suggests four ways in which this may come about, and the minister could have changed the language to avoid some of the traps he thinks are there, but essentially what we are saying to the minister is that there is a large number of fishermen who are not coadventurers in the sense in which he describes them in his amendment to the law, but are co-adventurers in another sense. At the request of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni I read the minutes of the parliamentary committee and the discussion between the member and Mr. Mitchell from the minister's department. As a lawyer as well as Member of Parliament, I am really at a loss to understand the basis of Mr. Mitchell's argument. Surely, the situation is this. The entire labour code is applicable only to those areas of activity which come under federal jurisdiction. Anything that is in the labour code which goes beyond that is therefore ultra vires. It is still understood in the law in the many cases that have come before the courts that our federal Labour Code, under its previous name as well as its present name, applies only to industrial activities or operations, whatever you want to call them, which come under federal jurisdiction.
That is how the minister is saddled with the longshoremen's problem in Montreal. Some years ago there were cases before the courts in which stevedoring companies took the position that all the activities connected with stevedoring that take place as they do in Toronto, Montreal, Trois-Rivieres or Quebec, come under provincial jurisdiction. I forget the name of the case, but it is there and the minister's advisers can find it. That case went to the Supreme Court of Canada which held that in view of the specific provisions in Section 91 of the British North America act, making shipping and related matters federal, all the operations which relate to or are connected with shipping operations come under federal jurisdiction. That is how the poor minister is now loaded with the problems of the longshoremen. There was an argument as to whether it came under federal jurisdiction and the Supreme Court of Canada ruled that since it was connected with an
Canada Labour Code
operation which was specifically under a heading in Section 91 of the BNA Act, it was federal. I say to him that fishing is under a specific heading, I forget which one, in Section 91 of the BNA Act. Therefore, if he accepts this amendment he would be in no different position from the one he would be in as a result of the amendment he has proposed.
I cannot understand the legal argument that was made because the amendment he proposed will be constitutional only to the extent it is held that co-adventuring operations in which fishermen participate come under federal jurisdiction. In the same way, the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni would be constitutional to the extent that the operations of fishermen there defined come under federal jurisdiction. What in heaven's name is the difficulty?
The minister cannot now decide whether these operations will come under provincial or federal jurisdiction. I say to him in all kindness that it is impossible for Mr. Mitchell or anyone else to make that decision, because that decision can only be made by the courts after they have heard the facts of the case, after they have had before them all the facts of the relationship regarding the operation and the facts regarding the way in which the fishing is done. That is the only way a decision can be made. It cannot be made in the abstract, and I am surprised that the legal advisers are trying to make it in that way.
Let me repeat again my plea that the minister reconsider, because I am bold enough to suggest that the legal advice he has given needs at least a second look. The legal principle is not different as between the amendment he proposed and the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. As far as the legal principle is concerned there is no difference. Either both of them are unconstitutional or both are constitutional, and I think they are the latter. They are constitutional only to the extent that a court would hold the operations being carried on are operations under federal jurisdiction because of the presence of fishing under a specific heading in Section 91 of the BNA Act.
It is really just as simple as that at this stage. It may be very complicated later if a buyer of fish, for example, challenges it and goes to court. That may be a complicated case, but I suggest to the minister, and I am putting it strongly, that it is wrong for him to decide in the abstract now that his hands are tied. There are many things which have been passed by Parliament and by our legislatures which have gone to the courts and which the courts have said are ultra viries. This would not be the first time that has been done. That result has come about following some legislation. I do not think the minister is right in deciding that in this case he will make this decision now concerning its constitutionality, instead of taking the position that he wants to extend this law to the fishermen of Canada so that they may have advantage of the Labour Code and collective bargaining. He should extend it within the parameter of the constitutional provisions and let the courts decide on that parameter as no doubt they would do.

June 30, 1972
Canada Labour Code
The merchants of fishing are a pretty tough lot and they may take the matter to court. It may be that the minister's argument will lose. We do not guarantee that it will win. However, I suggest the minister really is being misled in his view in deciding that he cannot now have this House pass this amendment, because I am confident in my own mind that in some areas this amendment would stand up as valid, just as I think there are possibly other areas in which the amendment would not stand up as valid. That would depend entirely on the decision of the courts. I repeat that the minister cannot make that decision when he does not have the facts. That decision can be made only on the facts of each case and to make that decision in abstract is a disservice to the fishermen. He cannot, in my opinion get away with dealing with some of them and not dealing with the others. In legal principle, both are in the same boat if I may put it that way. I earnestly appeal to the minister and say to him that I believe this is an important matter for the fishermen.
Since the minister has agreed to take a partial step, he ought to take the complete step and not be, as the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) would put it, pusillanimous about it. He should take a chance and let the courts decide. If the courts should knock him down, he would not be the first minister to be knocked down by the courts.

It seems to me the whole situation has changed, particularly in respect of western fishing. I have listened to the argument of Homer Stevens for many years now. It seems to me that as a result of the license changes and the assistance we have given in terms of
June 30, 1972

developing very large canneries on the west coast, where we have in effect amalgamated all the facilities, we have made it impossible for most fishermen to own their own boats. We have amalgamated them into what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) would call a more viable industry. We have made so many changes that the people who are engaged in the fishing industry on the west coast are having considerable difficulty in labour relations or in understanding whether or not the fact that they are fishing from the boat means that they are employees of the man who owns the boat, employees of the man who buys the fish or, as the minister said, co-adventurers.
I know nothing about the law but I think it is not my job as a legislator, and I suggest it is not the job of the Minister of Labour as a legislator, to decide whether or not the Supreme Court, under a given circumstance would make a favourable decision. But I do suggest that we have an obligation to meet the condition as we see it today, and to draft legislation that will solve that problem. So far as I am concerned if the Supreme Court decides that we were wrong, then we have an obligation to come before Parliament again and change the legislation to accomplish what we wanted to do in the first place. If the Supreme Court says that it must be done in another way, we should pass amending legislation.
The role of the legislator is to solve the problems of the people whom he represents, and in this case those who are engaged in the fishing industry are in serious difficulty. They are in a totally unique industry in which the Unemployment Insurance Commission has had to make all kinds of exceptions. There are other industries in the same position, but it seems to me that until cabinet ministers decide, after hearing the advice, that they know the problem, until they make up their minds to introduce legislation that will solve the particular problems affecting the Canadian people without always looking with one eye at the civil servants, who obviously feel that they would be in a bad position if they recommended any course which would not be upheld by the Supreme Court, we have to press the Supreme Court to make decisions. If the Supreme Court is the viable body that it must be in making final judgments it will also look at modern, up-to-date conditions rather than attempt to interpret the legislation in a cold and distant way. I suggest that we should press the Supreme Court to make decisions and in this way our constitution will be viable and up-to-date.
If the minister will not even introduce legislation that will enable the Supreme Court to make a favourable decision, then he is less than responsible and certainly not very adventurous.

speechtext:
I just want to address myself again to the legal point which the minister raised. It is the advice which he received that makes me so upset about the decision he made. If Mr. Mitchell or any of the minister's other advisors are in the gallery, I hope they will forgive me for speaking frankly, as I do. What the minister has said, and what the argument of Mr. Mitchell was as I read it in the committee's proceeding, is that they are probably dealing with a person, using "person" in a legal sense, namely a company, that does no more than purchase and sell the fish or does no more than process the fish. What right has the minister or his advisers to make that decision? If those are the facts in a particular case, if the company in fact has nothing to do with the fishing operation, then there may be constitutional difficulties, although I would not be certain of it even in that case. But in the modern fishing industry and in other industries as well, those are not always the facts. A company that purchases or processes is often very likely to have made some kind of capital advance to the owner of the vessel or may even own the vessel or may have some kind of business arrangement with the people who operate the vessel.
There are all sorts of sets of facts that may come before the Court. We are dealing in this case, as in many other cases, with an integrated industry, and frequently the buyer and the processor have an interest in the fishing operation in one form or another. For all the minister knows, he may find cases, and I have read about them in the law books when I practiced labour law, where the company has the authority to decide who will be master of the vessel and to decide who will be hired to operate the vessel. I say to the minister that these things are not simple. They are complex sets of facts, and I can visualize a situation where it would be possible to persuade the court that the particular set of facts in that situation, the involvement of the purchaser and the processor in the fishing operation, is such as to make him a fishing employer for the purpose of this act.
This is the situation, and the minister is really running away from his responsibility by taking the advice which he has been given on the basis that this is a simple factual situation. Well, it ain't, Mr. Speaker, if I may use that well known Oxonian term. These things are not like that at all. In labour relations, with regard to the constitutional problem, there have been cases which have turned on the facts of the case, cases which may appear to the minister or to me to be very similar which have gone in the other direction because of facts which were brought before the court. I say to the minister that there is nothing in the situation that would justify his acceptance of the advice which he has been given, there is nothing that would justify his assumption of facts which have not been tested, and I think that his duty is to enable all the fishermen to come under the Labour Code now that he has taken that step. I congratulate him for taking it. I am very pleased that he has done so, and so is the hon. member for Comox-Alber-ni (Mr. Barnett) and all my other colleagues.
I suggest to the minister that it is his duty to take this step and to let each case depend on its facts. The courts will decide. There is nothing humbling or humiliating about this Parliament saying that we want the fishermen covered by this law and then finding that in some cases
Some bon. Members: Agreed.

June 30, 1972
Canada Labour Code
the courts say they are not covered by this law because the law to that extent is invalid. To assume that a particular company carries on certain operations and therefore cannot possibly be involved in the fishing operation is a false assumption; it is just not factual. The facts will be the basis of any court decision, and the minister should not make the decision without giving the court a chance, and without giving the fishermen a chance, to fight their case in court. Let them go to court and fight the case. It will not be up to the minister to fight it. In any problem like that, even though the constitutional argument may be involved, it is not necessarily the Attorney General of Canada or of a province who is involved because they are usually given notice so they can be there if they want to, but it is not necessarily they who carry the case. In this case it will be the fishermen and the alleged employer who will carry the case. I do not think the minister should take from the fishermen the opportunity to fight their cases through the courts. Some cases they will lose and some they will win, and those that they win will be very important for the people involved.
Again, I appeal to the minister not to rest on the advice he has received. Since we are almost at one o'clock, and if the minister is ready to reconsider, we might call it one o'clock to give him another opportunity to discuss it with his advisers. But if he is not ready to reconsider it, what can one do?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is one of the more interesting sections in the entire bill. First, we would be faced with a situation that we did not have to be concerned about in the present labour bill inasmuch as we have brought into play the results of technological change and its effects upon employer and employee.
Canada Labour Code
I should like to say that notwithstanding what we may do regarding the bill presently before us management and labour, particularly labour leaders, must realize that it is important and necessary for them to have at least three criteria in order to save the whole collective bargaining process. I shall elaborate on them in this way.
First, we cannot continue to have the collective bargaining process involved with confrontation rather than negotiation. It is necessary that the parties realize that the third party involved in the collective bargaining agreement, that is the Canadian public, is becoming very involved in them even though it does not sit at the bargaining table. It is, therefore, incumbent upon labour and management to bargain in good faith and this should be one of the foundations of the whole system. At the present time I do not think that employers and labour leaders are bargaining in good faith.
The second criteria to be met is that the two parties should approach the bargaining table from flexible positions. We will never get anywhere unless they do.
The third criteria would provide for full disclosure. There is no point in going to the bargaining table unless all the facts are put on the table so that solutions can be arrived at which will benefit the employee, the employer and, more important, the third party.
When this bill was first introduced as Bill C-253, there was a great furor and cries of dismay and despair. And rightly so, Mr. Speaker, because in the first place, there were no escape clauses. There was no way for management and labour to decide by themselves whether they could reach the type of agreement that this bill calls for in terms of the effect of technological change, so in its wisdom the government introduced another bill. And this is where we come in now, Mr. Speaker, at clause 149, which I refer to as the escape section.
There are three instances, and I shall not elaborate upon them, in which the parties would not have to rely on clauses 150, 152 and 153, which are the basic clauses dealing with technological change, if, first, notice is given prior to entering into a particular collective agreement. The second escape clause is, of course, 149(2)(b), which reads:
the collective agreement contains provisions that specify procedures by which any matters that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment likely to be affected by a technological change may be negotiated and finally settled during the term of the agreement;
As I understand it, Mr. Speaker, there was some question whether these two clauses were disjunctive. We now know that is so and we have two escape provisions so far. The third escape provision is the one referred to in clause 149(2)(c) which reads as follows:
the collective agreement contains provisions that
(i)	are intended to assist employees affected by any technological change to adjust to the effects of the technological change; and
(ii)	specify that sections 150, 152 and 153 do not apply, during the term of the collective agreement, to the employer and the bargaining agent.

June 30, 1972
Canada Labour Code
What concerns me, and this is the gist of my motion, is that subclause (c) is not just junk. I pose this question because it seems that within subclause (2)(c) you have some groundwork whereby if the parties in the collective agreement can bring about some formulae which are intended to assist employers affected by technological change to adjust to the technological change, that should stand by itself and rightly so. If two parties can sit down and say this is what we will have in our agreement in order to show an intention of what labour and management desire in terms of the effects of technological change, why can it not stand by itself? The government says no, we cannot do it that way; we have to bring in the words "and acquire a waiver".
This is the part that not only bothers me, but many on this side of the House as well as many on the other side of the House. The government says you can make such an agreement, but at the same time you must acquire a waiver. In this regard, a waiver of the provisions of clauses 150, 152 and 153 is a further burden on the negotiating process inasmuch as management will have to attempt to buy that labour in order for it to have any meaningful contract in the long run. On the other hand, as it has been explained to me, the union will in turn have to go back to its membership and say, before we can enter into an agreement under this particular section, we must get your permission to exclude a waiver of something which is legally yours. This places the union in a very peculiar situation, a situation which they do not accept nor want.
Why can the second portion of subclause (c) not stand by itself? In other words, instead of having the word "and", why can it not read, "or specify that clauses 150, 152 and 153 do not apply". What is wrong with leaving that decision to labour and management? Surely they can, through any means which they can conceive and devise, say they will agree to this; we do not have to worry about the technological change because we know what is going to happen; we can guarantee security, jobs or anything that affects the employee without having to go into the act. It should be their right to say that they can opt out of the technological change sections of this bill.
There are a lot of reasons for asking the government why they are now imposing this particular section on labour and management when, in effect, technological change and its effects should be something that is settled around the bargaining table. There is a great concern in management. I could read off many other points of concern, but I do not want to waste the time of the House. They are afraid of harrassment. They are worried that there will be more negotiations, more strikes, unnecessary government interference, as they call it, double jeopardy, planning difficulty and disclosure of the technological change. They have every right to be concerned. The concern would be minimized if we could be assured that labour and management would approach the bargaining table in good faith, with flexible positions and make full disclosure. I am trying to arrive at industrial peace. That calls for the opportunity of the parties opting out of the technological change section. It is not a difficult argument
to follow. It just depends on whether the government believes there is some merit in this type of argument.
I am concerned about the technological section. If we relate our thoughts to the present situation of a Montreal port strike, we have a labour bill, a collective agreement, an arbitrator who has handed down a decision, union leadership and the wishes of Parliament as expressed through the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) all being ignored. Even if we pass this bill, it probably will not have any effect because of the attitude that some union leaders have taken that they are expressing the wishes and desires of the whole trade union movement. I disagree with this. There is one thing we have to be concerned about, and that is the public interest.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSION AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSION AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
The public interest must prevail no matter what the two parties may be thinking or may conclude. As Parliamentarians, it is our job to step in when the public interest is being adversely affected. Certainly, the collective bargaining process is the best process so far, but we have to question it at this time because it is not working. What I am trying to do with my amendment is make it work because with the imposition of the technological change section and the resultant ultimate need to reopen a contract that has already been duly signed, there is a great fear. If no agreement can be reached, there will be a strike. This is what many people fear. The Canadian people would be concerned if they knew that that is the principle behind this bill.
The polls are giving us some indication that governments must be responsible. I am not talking only about this government. I do not intend to be partisan this afternoon. I have a charitable spot in my heart because I hope we are going home. Here is an opportunity to show that we are bringing in an innovation, something that has never happened before, whereby a collective agreement which has been duly signed can be reopened if there is a disagreement and the possibility of a strike. This is what many people are concerned about in 1972.
All I am trying to do is look at the situation and throw in another escape clause. I think the parties are entitled to it. When two parties come to an agreement, they can say this is what we intend to do if technological changes affect a significant number of people within any organization. They make their decision and the contract is closed. On the other hand, if the union and labour can make some arrangement whereby they can maintain the security that employees are rightly seeking without having any recourse to this bill, why can they not do that? That is what I am talking about. This clause, together with clauses 150, 151, 152 are the clauses of the bill on which the most emphasis has been placed.
There is some talk about the balance of power. I do not know who, in fact, has the balance of power, but I do not want to talk about that. I want to talk about what is good for the Canadian people. This bill can only be good for the Canadian people if there are enough escape clauses in it in order that the true collective bargaining process can be left to those who are directly involved. We cannot sit idly by and hope things will get better. There are indications right now that things are not going well with the collective
(Mr. Alexander.]
June 30, 1972

bargaining process. Here is an ideal opportunity to relieve some of the fears of both management and labour. The clause will work much better, if amended, because there will be more avenues through which to proceed. If better prospects for industrial peace are what we want, I respectfully suggest that hon. members give this motion profound thought.
We cannot afford industrial strife and subsequent strikes leading only to unemployment and lost markets. Right now there is a strike in progress which is costing Montreal, I have heard, $1 million a day. And that is only an estimate for Montreal itself. Heaven knows what it is costing the Province of Quebec or, indirectly, the Province of Ontario, the rest of Canada and western Canada in particular through its affect on the grain trade. It is bound to be an astronomical figure. With these things in mind we should attempt to amend the bill so that its shortcomings are corrected to some extent. This is all I am asking-that sub-clause (c) should use the word "but", making it disjunctive, rather than the word "and" whose presence would result in a most complicated process being followed.
You see, Mr. Speaker, the unions will not ask for a waiver. They could not get one, because their membership would not agree. So they will rely upon subclause (b) or upon subclause (a). Thus, instead of having three options available the number of options will in practice be reduced to two. I am trying to ensure that there will be all three as intended by the minister. Why should the unions ask for a waiver? Why should they ask to be relieved of their rights? Unless the disjunctive word "but" is introduced, the subclause will not work. All I am trying to do is to get some sense into this bill and have a clause which would have some chance of working.
I have attempted, to the best of my ability, to present the motion and explain the reasoning behind it. I now hope that hon. members, after some debate, will accept the proposition I have put before them and vote in its favour.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSION AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a few words in support of the proposition which the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) has so eloquently placed before the House. This is probably the most important motion before us today.
As my hon. friend has said, industrial relations at the present time could be a great deal better than they are. The general public is dissatisfied with the way in which collective bargaining is working. They fear their interests are being completely overlooked in the course of the continuing battle between management and labour. One would have thought that at a time like this, in the course of the critical situation facing the Port of Montreal, any government would hesitate before doing anything which might in any way heighten the tension which exists between the two parties to a labour dispute. One might think that any government worthy of the name would be solely concerned about bringing in legislation which would lessen the tension between the two parties to a dispute, that it would introduce changes to the Labour Code designed to lessen mistrust and antagonism between the parties involved.
Canada Labour Code
Reading the preamble to this bill one receives the impression that the government did intend to do something to improve industrial relations. The last paragraph reads:
And whereas the Parliament of Canada desires to continue and extend its support to labour and management in their co-operative efforts to develop good relations and constructive collective bargaining practices, and deems the development of good industrial relations to be in the best interests of Canada in ensuring a just share of the fruit of progress to all-
This would encourage one to believe that something was contained in the legislation which would improve the bargaining process. Mr. Speaker, when the forerunner to this legislation, Bill C-253, was introduced it was immediately attacked both by management and by organized labour. It was criticized by management because of the clause concerning technological change to which my hon. friend has referred. This clause was included, ostensibly, to give both parties a better basis upon which to bargain. But according to management, instead of improving relations it would damage relations between the parties. It might be said that management has certain vested interests and, of course, this is true. But regardless of this aspect, the clause is disliked by management, whether its position is right or wrong. Thus, rather than contributing to the lessening of tension, such a provision could only contribute to the growing distrust between the parties. To me, this is the most objectionable feature of the bill.
I have read the briefs and I am aware of the representations which have been made. In the circumstances, I am amazed that the minister can be so intransigent. He refuses to compromise. He says, in effect: This is what I have decided and this is what you will get. My hon. friend, in his wisdom, has suggested a way out which may appease one side at the bargaining table and which will certainly not damage the other. I think the provisions are strong enough. We are now entering a new area of bargaining and destroying the sacrosanct nature of a contract. We are saying that under certain conditions contracts can be broken. It seems to me that if you are bargaining in good faith and arrive at a contract, both parties to the contract should be bound by it. It is very disturbing to see a situation exist in this country today in which parties to a contract not only refuse to honour the contract but refuse to obey the law, and publicly so state, in which event, to use a common phrase, the contract is not worth the paper it is written on.
What is the point of trying to legislate for co-operation and for bargaining in good faith? Legislation cannot produce that. You must convince parties to an agreement that both must act and bargain in good faith. Unless that is done all the legislation in the world will not make them reach an agreement that either of them would respect. That is the dangerous part of this clause. I should like to see the entire clause deleted. It is amusing to sit in committee and listen to various witnesses and departmental officials say that most contracts now contain provisions to cushion the effects of technological change, but that because there is the odd employer who does not agree to such provision the government must bring in an allembracing clause like this and thus drag everybody into

June 30, 1972
Canada Labour Code
the net. In my opinion, this kind of provision endangers the entire collective bargaining process.
I think we should admit that we have given up trying to get the government to withdraw completely the clauses dealing with technological change. But in all fairness to both parties to a dispute the government should be prepared to accept the amendment that has been put forward by my colleague which provides one more opportunity for two parties to reach agreement. Mr. Speaker, I rise for just a moment or two to express the hope that on this occasion the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) will not be pusillanimous. I hope that he will reject this amendment. As I see it, what we are dealing with in global terms at this point is the whole business of writing a technological change provision into the labour code. We think it ought to be there, that it ought to be stronger, but at least there should be support for it in the legislation as far as it goes.
What we are dealing with in the immediate amendment to the escape provisions of the bill is an attempt to make it possible under certain conditions for the technological change provisions not to apply. Clause 149(2) provides a set of conditions under which the technological change provisions need not apply. The one in particular that is dealt with by the amendment moved by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) is a two-part escape provision providing, in effect, that the technological change provisions do not apply if both of two other provisions are written into a collective agreement: one, a provision intended to assist employees in the event of technological change; two, specific recognition of the fact that the technological change provisions of the bill do not apply.
I suggest that if you change the "and" to "or", you will make the escape clause that much wider. You will make it possible for the technological change provisions not to apply, on the very flimsy ground that there can be found in the agreement provisions which might seem to assist employees affected by technological change. The provisions in this whole area of the bill are weak enough as they are that I do not think that they should be weakened further. speakeroldname: Hon. Martin P. O'Connell (Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSION AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this discussion we are again at the very heart of the Labour Code. A very important section of the bill is clauses 149 to 153. These provisions bring into the collective bargaining process the impact on employees of technological change. The object of these clauses we are currently debating is to ensure that the provisions are viable in the administrative sense, that they do contribute to constructive industrial relations, and that they bring about equity as between the two parties.
I was very interested in the case made by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) as they strug-

gled with this, as indeed the standing committee did over an extended period. I am not adopting a position of intransigence, but I am not able to compromise on these provisions, as suggested to me, since what has been suggested as the compromise would undermine my view of constructive industrial relations as they bear upon technological change.
It has been suggested that we make paragraph (i) and paragraph (ii) disjunctive. At the moment the two paragraphs are connected with an "and", which it is suggested we change to "or". In my opinion, the effect of that change would jeopardize agreements that are made between employers and employees and would, from the employers' point of view, expose them to a reopening of the bargaining to which they have been party. If we accepted the amendment we would indeed open the door to the reopening of collective agreements after they had been sealed with the intention that they remain sealed.
What we have been trying to do in constructing the sections of the bill that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre described as escape clauses is truly to make agreements final from the point of view of equity between the two parties. There must be a seal on the agreement, and the only way to seal it is to leave the word "and" connecting paragraph (i) and paragraph (ii) of subclause (c) of clause 149(2).
Let us consider what would undoubtedly happen when a technological change occurs in a situation where an employer and the employees have agreed upon a substantive provision to deal with it. Let us assume we are in the position the hon. member for Hamilton West suggested, and we have made this disjunctive. The bargaining agent may take the position before the Canada Labour Relations Board that he has provision for technological change as a result of bargaining, but not for this particular change. He may say the union did not contemplate this change when they made the bargain, and this is an extraordinary change which is going to significantly affect in an adverse manner a number of employees. There would be constant litigation in that event before the Canada Labour Relations Board, because the parties would not have sealed the bargain and said for the term of the agreement, two years or three years, they had provided for technological change with these substantive provisions and, as risky as it may be, they are acting in good faith.
The bargaining agent may say to the employer that the union has bargained for these provisions and will live with them for that period without opening the agreement or running to the Labour Relations Board to plead that this was not the kind of thing about which they were thinking.

speechtext: They don't need this act.

speechtext:
They do need the act. If they have made these provisions, they should be protected against reopening, and it is the "and" that protects them. The provisions are there, and the parties agree that those provisions are sufficient for the purposes of this act for this period of time. I am sure it is not in the mind of the hon. member for Hamilton West or the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) to expose agreements to reopening. They simply see the difficulty in the ordinary course of bargaining. I agree there will be difficulty, but that is why there are bargaining agents.
I think the hon. member for Hamilton West said these are issues for the bargaining table. I certainly agree they are, and that is the place to settle them. That is where assurance should be given the employers, just as it is given the employees, that these are bargains struck in good faith.
I said in opening that to make this administratively feasible we need the "and", so the Canada Labour Relations Board is not continuously drawn into litigation over whether this provision did in fact deal adequately with the situation. Without the "and" what would the question before the board be? The bargaining agent could then say they have some provisions but they are not adequate to cover a certain change. We have then transferred the question of adequacy away from the bargaining table and put it before the board. The board should not be drawn into this kind of question at all. We say to the parties, if you bargain for these then seal them, close the matter and accept it but do not ask another agency to enter into bargaining and tell you whether you have done an adequate job.
From an administrative and an equity point of view I suggest the "and" is necessary. The employer would undoubtedly trade the technological change provisions for the non-reopener clause. He does not want things reopened. From the point of view of the trade union in accepting these provisions, it must have known that the
Canada Labour Code
employer offered the provision to the union in order to get a closed contract. Having gone through all that, it would not contribute to constructive industrial relations to then leave an opening for reopening because of the inadequacy of the deal that was arrived at. That would create a situation which I do not think any of us would want.
In closing, let me say again that this was thoroughly reviewed in the committee. I have spent many hours considering this and discussing it with employers and associations of employers. I have discussed it with trade unionists as well. Many hon. members, particularly those on this side from British Columbia, have made a very strong plea and presented a very cogent case during the number of occasions I have met with them. They have a particular interest because employers on the west coast have put a strong case to them. I feel very strongly that I would be letting down the employers as well as the trade unionists if I gave in on this point. At the risk of being what is called intransigent, I must ask the House to resist the amendment before it and accept the original proposal advanced in the bill.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I had some considerable discussion in the committee with regard to the principle advocated in this amendment. It also represents the heart and core of private bills I have presented in this House since 1969. In 1971, the bill was known as C-138.1 shall not go through a recital of the other numbers. However, they stem from the Hoogendorn case in Ontario and similar instances of that kind in the province of British Columbia, in my own province of Alberta and I am sure other provinces. As an individual, I was absolutely repelled and amazed that here, in Canada we would allow to happen what happened in those cases. These cases involve the fact that, by reason of conscience, a man or woman objects to belonging to either a closed shop or a union shop organization. Such a person does not believe in that type of unionism. This is a matter of true conscience. Yet, the effect of the closed shop and the union shop is that such an individual cannot maintain his or her employment.
This might involve the case of an individual who had worked in some undertaking which was not unionized, and then later the work force became organized. He or she is forced to belong to the union and to pay dues to the union in order to maintain employment in complete contradiction of that person's bona fide religious beliefs. That is why I have put forward this motion. I suggest the Labour Code is in fact contrary to the Canadian Bill of Rights, insofar as it says to unions that they can deprive individuals of their work because of their religious beliefs. I am not arguing here the validity or otherwise or the justification or otherwise of the religious belief held by the individual. I may say, however, that there are many people of the Reform Church in this country who do not believe in this. In addition, I have before me a letter from the General Counsel of the Seventh-day Adventist Church in Canada. For the benefit of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) who argued against me on this matter, may I say that this letter comes from the executive offices of that church in Oshawa. I want to read the letter:
The members of our communion have long felt that closed shop and union shop contracts in many instances force them to belong to unions when their conscientious convictions prevent them from

doing so. The provision that your bill would make in the federal legislation would certainly meet this problem.
Seventh-day Adventists do not wish to enjoy the benefits that come from the work of trade unionists and trade unions. However, some of the methods employed by trade unions in achieving their goals are such that conscientious Christians with strong views against the resort to violence and intimidation find themselves in a difficult position. They are prepared to make a contribution equivalent to union dues to some charity of the union's choice and even go so far as to have the union get credit for this contribution. They would appreciate the opportunity to work, in return, without in any way frustrating or thwarting the legitimate aims of their fellow employees who happen to be members of a trade union. But, neither do they wish to be forced to join an association or organization where conscientious scruples prevent them from doing so.
I hear snorts of disbelief from the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby who I say, frankly, epitomizes to my way of thinking some of the worst features of big unionism in his attitude toward this matter.
While I may not agree with the Quakers or others who for reasons of conscience do not accept that they should bear arms in service of our country, yet we accord them this privilege. They enjoy the full benefit of membership in Canadian society. It is asserted that because these individuals about whom I am concerned share some of the benefits-not all because the unions do not get all the benefits on behalf of their workers even though they believe they do-they must make their contribution and must belong. It is suggested that they should be grateful to belong. Since there is a limited amount of time, I wish to read and place on the record what is stated in the Canadian Bill of Rights. I shall read, first of all, from the preamble:
The Parliament of Canada, affirming that the Canadian Nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge the supremacy of God, the dignity and worth of the human person and the position of the family in a society of free men and free institutions:
I would reiterate the acknowledgement of the supremacy of God, the dignity and worth of the human person and the position of the family in a society of free men and free institutions. That is something many people appear to wish to deny today. The quotation continues:
Affirming also that men and institutions remain free only when freedom is founded upon respect for moral and spiritual values and the rule of law;
I commend those words to hon. members, and particularly to those who wish to steamroller individuals who would dissent.
And being desirous of enshrining these principles and the human rights and fundamental freedoms derived from them, in a Bill of Rights which shall reflect the respect of Parliament for its constitutional authority and which shall ensure the protection of these rights and freedoms in Canada:
Then, the following is enacted:
1.	It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely:
(a)	the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the
person and the enjoyment of property, and the right not to be
deprived thereof except by due process of law;
This is the provision regarding the right to work. Then, we have paragraph 2:
2.	Every law of Canada shall, unless it is expressly declared by an Act of the Parliament of Canada that it shall operate notwith-
June 30, 1972

standing the Canadian Bill of Rights, be so construed and applied as not to abrogate, abridge or infringe or to authorize the abrogation, abridgment or infringement of any of the rights or freedoms herein recognized and declared,
Then, there is a particularization, but no limitation. Part II, section 5 (1) reads:
Nothing in Part I shall be construed to abrogate or abridge any human right or fundamental freedom not enumerated therein that may have existed in Canada at the commencement of this Act.
Then, sub-sections (2) and (3) state:
(2) The expression 'law of Canada' in Part I means an Act of the Parliament of Canada enacted before or after the coming into force of this Act, any order, rule or regulation thereunder, and any law in force in Canada or in any other part of Canada at the commencement of this Act that is subject to be repealed, abolished or altered by the Parliament of Canada.
3.	The provisions of Part I shall be construed as extending only to matters coming within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada.
It is clear to my mind that, in so far as the Canada Labour Code refuses to recognize the right of the individual as propounded in the amendment, it is an infringement of the Canadian Bill of Rights. The government of Ontario in 1970 amended its labour code and put in section 35(a) to take care specifically of the point that I have put forward. Unfortunately, I think the government of Ontario did not go far enough because this provision indicates that if an individual joins an organization where there is a collective agreement in force, and it is one of a closed shop or union shop nature, the act shall not apply to that person. But in effect I say that the rights granted under the Ontario amendment of 1970 are more illusory than they are real.
I say that we should recognize the principle that there is a freedom of conscience, a freedom of religion. There has to be something that is real, or do we just pay lip service to it? I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the failure of the government to include such an amendment as I have put forward, or a provision to accomplish the same end, means that the government is paying less than lip service to the rights of Canadian workers as enumerated under the Canadian Bill of Rights.
I hope that the House accepts my amendment. If it does not, I can promise hon. members that I will be back next year with a similar type of amendment if I am a private member. This is a matter that goes to the heart and core of labour law in this country. After all, so many of the people who belong to the party on my left talk about the right of individuals to dissent from the political views of the government and of other people, but when it comes to conforming to union law there is no right to dissent.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate, but my hon. friend who is figuratively and literally on my right has
Canada Labour Code
provoked me to say a few words in support of the bill as it now stands and contrary to the amendment that is supported by the Conservative party. I would like to come to grips with what I think is the essential philosophical point of dispute here, and that concerns something called one's conscience.
The argument offered by the hon. member who preceded me was that the state must take into full recognition the obligations that one imposes upon oneself because of conscience. I say to the hon. member with all respect that never in my studies of philosophy and ethics have I had much intellectual respect for that kind of argument. I will tell the House why. If you study history you will find that the most scandalous deeds ever performed were often performed by men who claimed they acted in conscience. Men who have performed the most vile and inhuman practices in human history almost invariably have said they did them according to conscience, and indeed in many cases I would be prepared to accept that they were acting according to conscience; in other words, that they were doing what they deemed to be right and correct.
However, in any ethical decision it seems to me that one does not primarily consider motives but, rather, one has to consider the implications and the consequences for society as a whole and for other members of the group affected. For example, I could cite cases in medieval history of Catholics who thought it was entirely morally appropriate to torture, to put on the rack and to burn at the stake early Protestants because they as Catholics were acting in good conscience, they thought it was entirely appropriate and justified to so act.
Would we now sanction, in terms of our perception of morality, of our understanding of what is socially good, such activity? With respect, I would say no. One could cite in early renaissance history similar acts by Protestants who thought it was entirely appropriate and good to burn a Catholic every Thursday afternoon at three o'clock if they could get their hands on one. These Protestants in our history also thought they were acting in good conscience, and I would say with respect that they were acting in good conscience. It is simply a matter of ethical right and wrong, in my view, that their conscience was leading them to profoundly immoral acts.
In short, conscience is by no means a sufficient criterion to judge the goodness or badness of an act. Therefore, I submit that the argument put forward by the hon. member that conscience is to be relied upon, that conscience may lead one to a conclusion contrary to that which is proposed by this legislation, is without any serious philosophical justification. To cite a particularly horrendous and unrepresentative example, perhaps there were literally thousands of Germans in the 1930s who thought that the political actions of a man called Adolph Hitler were entirely good and appropriate, and that a German in good conscience could do nothing other than support the kind of policies that Hitler was advocating.

Therefore, we come to the matter at issue. If we dismiss the philosophical argument of the conscience, and accept the utilitarian argument that you

June 30, 1972
Canada Labour Code
have to look at social consequences, then it seems to me that the legislation before us, and not the amendment, must be supported.
I categorically reject the anti-union attitude of the hon. member who preceded me, because most unions in this country are democratic organizations and are very much concerned with improving the well-being of their members. To suggest that they are always, or even usually, dominated by so-called big trade union bosses misses the point of reality.
The point is that by passing this kind of amendment we would be saying to a member of a trade union that although in most instances it was the trade union that had led to the doubling of that person's income in recent years, that the union had got him benefits so that he could no longer be fired at the whim of his employer, that the union had succeeded in getting him paid holidays, that the union had done for working people what political democracy in this century had done for society as a whole-that is, it had brought a degree of civil rights and civil dignity to the working people in Canada-the member had no financial obligation to that organization if he deemed it to be a matter of conscience. We would be saying to the worker that if he thinks it is not a matter of philosophical commitment, then he does not have to support the union; he does not have to support the thousands of workers who preceded him, who had to strike, on many occasions in terribly bad weather, in order to attain the financial gains and civil liberties in the workplace that he now enjoys.
I for one will not support a measure that gives a worker the right to opt out of a union and no longer pay his share toward achieving very desirable social aims.This is analogous to saying to the citizen of a democratic state, "You no longer have an obligation to pay your taxes if as a matter of conscience you are in profound disagreement with the government." I dare say that some members of the Conservative party Eire in profound disagreement with the present government. Therefore, if we followed the logic of the hon. member who preceded me they would be under no obligation to pay taxes to such a perfidious regime.
If it is wrong to say that to a citizen of a democratic state, I say it is equally wrong to say to a member of a democratic union that he has a right not to pay his share if he disagrees with the union. I urge that the House strongly vote against this amendment.
